A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Pinaleno Mountain landscape is evolving at rates comparable to those of many other active orogens, with the caveat that the landscape’s evolution is being driven primarily by incision in the Gila River, which is a response to the tectonically driven subsidence of Safford and Sulphur Springs basins during the Miocene and early Pliocene.

the Pinaleno–Safford landscape is evolving in the absence of active extensional tectonic processes, and that the rates of landscape evolution over the last 4 m.y. have been driven by the interaction between upland erosion rates and the rates of incision by the Gila River.

the post-tectonic evolution of the Pinalenos and Safford basin has been driven by the combined effects of regional base-level fall, millennial-scale climate change, and the arrival of the Gila from upstream.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the post-tectonic evolution of the Pinalenos and Safford is not a simple story of regional uplift and subsequent incision.

the Pinaleno–Safford landscape has undergone a relatively slow and steady post-tectonic evolution over the past 2–4 m.y., and that the timing and rate of post-tectonics landscape development is not a simple function of the timing and rate at which axial incision occurs.
the Pinaleno upland and Safford basin system has been actively degrading for at least the past 4.5 m.y., and that the rates of erosion and incision have been relatively constant over this period.
